timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Hello, I am Dr. Bhaskar Shunai, Head of the Department of Periodics and Chief of Division
of Periodic Infectious Diseases at Manipul Hospital, Bangalore.
Of course, natural immunity is always better, but the thing is, in the natural immunity,
the child will suffer from the disease and then it will get the immunity.
And here, short of suffering, the child will get immunity.
For example, in chickenpox, by vaccinating, we can avoid the child contacting the chicken
pox.
But, if the child gets chickenpox, child will get a lifelong immunity.
But in the process, the child will suffer for 10 to 15 days with a lot of rashes, eaching,
fever.
And once the child gets out of it, it will get some scars and that will take few more
weeks to months to clear it.
And few of them can have some complications also.
Chickenpox, though the grandmother says that it comes and goes and nothing will happen,
but we have seen the worst complications of chickenpox.
For example, if the virus can travel into the brain and cause n-capillaries, it can affect
the hind brain of the child and cause what is called as a cerebralitis.
And it can affect the liver, it can affect the kidney, it can affect the heart and lungs
and any of the major organs it can affect and cause complications.
We cannot predict which child is going to develop the complications.
But here by vaccinating, you can avoid these complications also.
So in a natural immunity, child will suffer and then get the immunity at the end of it
and there is a risk of getting complications.
In vaccination, short of suffering, the child will get immunity without suffering.
That is the difference.

youtube_description:
Dr. Bhaskar Shenoy explains Is natural immunity better than vaccine acquired immunity?

Is natural immunity better than vaccine-acquired immunity? Join Dr. Bhaskar Shenoy as he explores this question in depth, discussing the mechanisms and effectiveness of both types of immunity. Learn about the differences between natural immunity, which occurs after infection with a pathogen, and vaccine-acquired immunity, which is induced by vaccination. Dr. Shenoy will also delve into the nuances of these immune responses, considering factors such as duration, strength, and breadth of protection. Gain a comprehensive understanding of the complexities surrounding immunity and make informed decisions about your health. Don't miss this insightful discussion with Dr. Bhaskar Shenoy, an expert in immunology and infectious diseases.
